title: Ἔρις καὶ ὅπλισις
titleEn: Strife and the Arming of Agamemnon — Iliad 11.1–121
part: Strife and the Arming of Agamemnon (11.1–121)
about: Dawn rises, and Zeus sends Strife to the Achaean ships; she stands by Odysseus’ ship in the middle of the line and shouts, and the Achaeans find war sweeter than going home. Agamemnon arms, piece by piece: greaves, the breastplate that Cinyras gave him, a sword, a shield with the Gorgon on it, a helmet and two spears, and Athena and Hera thunder to honour him. The foot-soldiers get to the ditch before the horsemen, Zeus sends bloody dew, and the Trojans gather round Hector, who shows like a star among clouds. The armies meet like reapers, Strife alone of the gods rejoices, and Zeus sits apart, looking on. At the hour the woodcutter eats, the Danaans break the line, and Agamemnon kills Bianor and Oileus and then two sons of Priam, Isus and Antiphus, once captured by Achilles. They die like the fawns of a hind under a lion, and the Trojans flee before the Argives.

sentences.t:
Ἠὼς δ’ ἐκ λεχέων παρ’ ἀγαυοῦ Τιθωνοῖο
ὄρνυθ’, ἵν’ ἀθανάτοισι φόως φέροι ἠδὲ βροτοῖσι·
sentences.l:
And Dawn from her bed, from beside noble Tithonus,
was rising, so that to the immortals she might bring light, and to mortals;
sentences.i: And Dawn rose from her bed beside noble Tithonus, to bring light to the immortals and to mortals alike;
sentences.n: Dawn is the goddess Ἠώς, and her bed is left ‘from beside’ Τιθωνοῖο, the epic genitive (-οιο = Attic -ου) of Tithonus; the Greek leaves the tie between them unsaid. λεχέων is the genitive plural of λέχος ‘bed’. ὄρνυθ’ is ὄρνυτο ‘was rising’ with no augment (the same line in the Odyssey has the augmented ὤρνυτο), and ἵν’ … φέροι, a purpose clause with the optative, is ‘so that she might bring’. φόως is the epic form of φῶς ‘light’, and ἀθανάτοισι and βροτοῖσι are epic datives plural. The line is the Odyssey’s dawn-line, and its English is kept; ἀγαυοῦ ‘noble’ is a stock epithet.

sentences.t:
Ζεὺς δ’ Ἔριδα προΐαλλε θοὰς ἐπὶ νῆας Ἀχαιῶν
ἀργαλέην, πολέμοιο τέρας μετὰ χερσὶν ἔχουσαν.
sentences.l:
And Zeus sent forth Strife to the swift ships of the Achaeans,
grievous, a portent of war in her hands holding.
sentences.i: Zeus sent forth grievous Strife to the swift ships of the Achaeans, holding in her hands a portent of war.
sentences.n: Ἔριδα is Strife, here a goddess who acts, so the name takes a capital. προΐαλλε ‘sent forth’ is the imperfect of προϊάλλω, with no augment. θοάς ‘swift’ is the stock epithet of ships. ἀργαλέην ‘grievous’ agrees with Ἔριδα, and μετὰ χερσὶν ἔχουσαν is ‘holding in her hands’. τέρας ‘portent’ is a sign sent by a god; the Greek does not say what Strife carries, only that it is a portent of war.

sentences.t:
στῆ δ’ ἐπ’ Ὀδυσσῆος μεγακήτεϊ νηῒ μελαίνῃ,
ἥ ῥ’ ἐν μεσσάτῳ ἔσκε γεγωνέμεν ἀμφοτέρωσε,
ἠμὲν ἐπ’ Αἴαντος κλισίας Τελαμωνιάδαο
ἠδ’ ἐπ’ Ἀχιλλῆος,
sentences.l:
and she stood by Odysseus’ huge black ship,
which was in the middle, to be heard on both sides,
both to the huts of Ajax, Telamon’s-son,
and to Achilles’,
sentences.i: She stood by the huge black ship of Odysseus, which lay in the middle, so that a shout carried in both directions, both to the huts of Ajax, son of Telamon, and to those of Achilles,
sentences.n: The subject is still Strife, and she takes her stand where a shout will carry furthest. Her place is Odysseus’ ship in the middle of the line, and γεγωνέμεν ‘to be heard’ with ἀμφοτέρωσε ‘on both sides’ says the sound reached both ends, ἐπ’ … κλισίας ‘to the huts’ of Ajax and of Achilles. Τελαμωνιάδαο is a patronymic, ‘son of Telamon’, with the epic genitive -αο. μεγακήτεϊ ‘huge’ is probably μέγα- + κῆτος ‘sea-monster’, but the formation is not secure. The lines about Odysseus’ ship stand at 8.222–225a, where Agamemnon is the one who ‘stood’, and their English is kept with ‘she’.

sentences.t:
τοί ῥ’ ἔσχατα νῆας ἐΐσας
εἴρυσαν ἠνορέῃ πίσυνοι καὶ κάρτεϊ χειρῶν
ἔνθα στᾶσ’ ἤϋσε θεὰ μέγα τε δεινόν τε
ὄρθι’,
sentences.l:
who at the farthest the well-balanced ships
had drawn up, trusting in manliness and in strength of hands;
there, having stood, she shouted, the goddess, greatly and fearsomely,
high-pitched,
sentences.i: who had drawn up their well-balanced ships at the farthest ends, trusting in their manliness and the strength of their hands; and there the goddess took her stand and shouted, greatly and fearsomely, in a high-pitched voice,
sentences.n: τοί ‘who’ are the men of Ajax and Achilles, whose ships lie at the two ends of the line; ἔσχατα ‘at the farthest’ is a neuter plural used as an adverb. εἴρυσαν is the augmented aorist of ἐρύω ‘draw up’ (haul ashore), its augment written ει-, ἐΐσας ‘well-balanced’ is the stock epithet of ships (its sense is not certain), ἠνορέῃ is ‘manliness’ and κάρτεϊ the epic dative of κράτος ‘strength’. After the relative clause the sentence picks up with ἔνθα στᾶσ’ ἤϋσε ‘there, having taken her stand, she shouted’ (στᾶσ’ the aorist participle of ἵστημι, ἤϋσε the augmented aorist of ἀΰω ‘shout’, with its diaeresis as printed). μέγα τε δεινόν τε are neuter adverbs, ‘greatly and fearsomely’; ὄρθια (here elided) is literally ‘upright’ and of a voice is usually taken as ‘high-pitched, shrill’. The relative clause (τοί … χειρῶν) stands at 8.225–226, and its English is kept. The unit stops at the comma.

sentences.t:
Ἀχαιοῖσιν δὲ μέγα σθένος ἔμβαλ’ ἑκάστῳ
καρδίῃ ἄληκτον πολεμίζειν ἠδὲ μάχεσθαι.
sentences.l:
and to the Achaeans great strength she put, to each
in the heart, unrelenting, to make war and to fight.
sentences.i: and she put great, relentless strength into the heart of every Achaean, for making war and fighting.
sentences.n: Ἀχαιοῖσιν ‘to the Achaeans’ is narrowed by ἑκάστῳ ‘to each’ and by καρδίῃ ‘in the heart’, all datives. ἔμβαλ’ is ἔμβαλε, ‘put into’, the aorist of ἐμβάλλω, without augment (Attic ἐνέβαλε); σθένος is ‘strength’. ἄληκτον ‘unrelenting’ (ἀ- + λήγω ‘cease’) agrees with σθένος, and the infinitives πολεμίζειν ἠδὲ μάχεσθαι ‘to make war and to fight’ say what the strength is for.

sentences.t:
τοῖσι δ’ ἄφαρ πόλεμος γλυκίων γένετ’ ἠὲ νέεσθαι
ἐν νηυσὶ γλαφυρῇσι φίλην ἐς πατρίδα γαῖαν.
sentences.l:
And to them straightway war became sweeter than to go back
in the hollow ships to their dear fatherland.
sentences.i: And at once war became sweeter to them than going home in their hollow ships to their dear fatherland.
sentences.n: Fighting is now sweeter than going home. τοῖσι ‘to them’ is the article used as a pronoun, the Achaeans; γλυκίων is the comparative of γλυκύς ‘sweet’, with ἠέ ‘than’, and νέεσθαι is the infinitive ‘to go back’. γένετ’ is ἐγένετο, unaugmented, and νηυσὶ γλαφυρῇσι is the epic dative plural ‘in the hollow ships’. These two lines stand at 2.453–454, and their English is kept.

sentences.t:
Ἀτρεΐδης δ’ ἐβόησεν ἰδὲ ζώννυσθαι ἄνωγεν
Ἀργείους·
sentences.l:
And Atreus’-son shouted, and bade gird themselves
the Argives;
sentences.i: The son of Atreus shouted and bade the Argives gird themselves;
sentences.n: Ἀτρεΐδης ‘son of Atreus’ is Agamemnon, who is not named until later in this part; the poet now calls the army Argives. ἰδέ is an epic ‘and’. ζώννυσθαι is the middle infinitive of ζώννυμι ‘gird’: to put on the belt, and with it the armour, so ‘arm themselves’. ἄνωγεν is a past tense of ἄνωγα ‘bid’, with Ἀργείους as its object; the unit stops at the raised dot, in the middle of the line.

sentences.t: ἐν δ’ αὐτὸς ἐδύσετο νώροπα χαλκόν.
sentences.l: and he himself put on the flashing bronze.
sentences.i: and he himself put on the flashing bronze.
sentences.n: ἐν … ἐδύσετο is tmesis (the preverb stands apart) for ‘put on’; ἐδύσετο is the epic aorist middle of δύω, with -σε- for -σα-. ‘Bronze’ means his bronze armour, and αὐτός ‘himself’ turns from the army to its leader. νώροπα ‘flashing’ is the traditional gloss of an adjective whose meaning is not known. The same words stand at 2.578, and their English is kept.

sentences.t:
κνημῖδας μὲν πρῶτα περὶ κνήμῃσιν ἔθηκε
καλὰς ἀργυρέοισιν ἐπισφυρίοις ἀραρυίας·
sentences.l:
Greaves first about his shins he set,
fine ones, with silver ankle-clasps fitted;
sentences.i: First he set fine greaves about his shins, fitted with silver ankle-clasps;
sentences.n: The arming begins with the greaves, which are shin-guards. κνημῖδας is the accusative plural, κνήμῃσιν the epic dative plural of κνήμη ‘shin’, and ἔθηκε ‘set’ is the aorist of τίθημι. καλάς ‘fine’ and ἀραρυίας ‘fitted’ (perfect participle of ἀραρίσκω) agree with the greaves; ἀργυρέοισιν ἐπισφυρίοις is ‘with silver ankle-clasps’, the clasps that fasten them. These two lines stand at 3.330–331 of Paris, and their English is kept.

sentences.t:
δεύτερον αὖ θώρηκα περὶ στήθεσσιν ἔδυνε,
τόν ποτέ οἱ Κινύρης δῶκε ξεινήϊον εἶναι.
sentences.l:
Second, in turn, a breastplate about his chest he put on,
which once to him Cinyras gave to be a guest-gift.
sentences.i: Second, he put on about his chest the breastplate that Cinyras had once given him as a guest-gift.
sentences.n: δεύτερον αὖ ‘second, in turn’ continues the list of the armour, as at 3.332. θώρηκα is the accusative of θώραξ ‘breastplate’, and ἔδυνε ‘put on’ is the imperfect of δύνω, a by-form of δύω. τόν is the article-pronoun serving as a relative, ‘which’, and οἱ is ‘to him’. Κινύρης is Cinyras, who the next lines place on Cyprus. ξεινήϊον εἶναι is ‘to be a guest-gift’, an infinitive of purpose; a ξεινήϊον is what a host gives his guest-friend.

sentences.t:
πεύθετο γὰρ Κύπρον δὲ μέγα κλέος οὕνεκ’ Ἀχαιοὶ
ἐς Τροίην νήεσσιν ἀναπλεύσεσθαι ἔμελλον·
sentences.l:
for he heard, to Cyprus, a great report, that the Achaeans
in ships to Troy were about to sail out;
sentences.i: for he had heard the great report that came to Cyprus, that the Achaeans were about to sail out to Troy in their ships;
sentences.n: γάρ explains the gift. πεύθετο is ἐπεύθετο, the imperfect of πεύθομαι (the epic by-form of πυνθάνομαι) ‘learn, hear’, without augment. Κύπρον δέ (printed as two words) has the suffix -δε of direction, ‘to Cyprus’, though ‘heard’ is not a verb of motion; the sense is that the report came to Cyprus and Cinyras heard it there. κλέος is here a ‘report’, what is heard, and οὕνεκ’ is ὅτι ‘that’, introducing what the report said. ἀναπλεύσεσθαι is the future infinitive of ἀναπλέω, with ἔμελλον ‘were about to’; ἀνα- is ‘up’, out to sea. νήεσσιν is the epic dative plural of ναῦς.

sentences.t: τοὔνεκά οἱ τὸν δῶκε χαριζόμενος βασιλῆϊ.
sentences.l: for that reason to him this he gave, gratifying the king.
sentences.i: That was why he gave it to him, to please the king.
sentences.n: τοὔνεκα is τοῦ ἕνεκα ‘for that reason’. οἱ ‘to him’ is the enclitic pronoun and τόν ‘it’ (the breastplate) the article used as a pronoun, and βασιλῆϊ, the epic dative of βασιλεύς, names the king as Agamemnon. χαριζόμενος ‘gratifying’ is the participle of χαρίζομαι; the Greek says only that the gift was meant to please the king, and not what Cinyras expected in return.

sentences.t:
τοῦ δ’ ἤτοι δέκα οἶμοι ἔσαν μέλανος κυάνοιο,
δώδεκα δὲ χρυσοῖο καὶ εἴκοσι κασσιτέροιο·
sentences.l:
Of it, indeed, ten strips there were of black kyanos,
and twelve of gold and twenty of tin;
sentences.i: It had ten strips of black kyanos, twelve of gold, and twenty of tin;
sentences.n: τοῦ ‘of it’ is the breastplate, and ἤτοι (one word in this edition) is ‘indeed’. οἶμοι are strips or bands laid on the breastplate; how they were made is not said. κύανος names some dark-blue material whose identity is not known (enamel, glass-paste and lapis have all been proposed), so it is left as ‘kyanos’; μέλανος is ‘black’. κασσίτερος is tin. ἔσαν is the epic ἦσαν ‘there were’, and the unit stops at the raised dot, after the tin.

sentences.t:
κυάνεοι δὲ δράκοντες ὀρωρέχατο προτὶ δειρὴν
τρεῖς ἑκάτερθ’ ἴρισσιν ἐοικότες, ἅς τε Κρονίων
ἐν νέφεϊ στήριξε, τέρας μερόπων ἀνθρώπων.
sentences.l:
And dark serpents reached up toward the neck,
three on each side, like rainbows, which the son of Cronus
in a cloud has fixed, a portent for speech-dividing men.
sentences.i: Dark serpents reached up toward the neck, three on each side, like rainbows, which the son of Cronus has set in a cloud as a portent for men of articulate speech.
sentences.n: κυάνεοι ‘dark’ is the adjective of the kyanos above; whether it says the serpents are made of that material is not said. ὀρωρέχατο is a pluperfect passive of ὀρέγω ‘stretch’ in the ending -ατο (= -ντο), ‘had been stretched out’, so ‘reached up’; προτὶ δειρήν is ‘toward the neck’. ἴρισσιν is the epic dative plural of ἶρις ‘rainbow’, and ἐοικότες is ‘like’. ἅς τε, with epic τε, begins a general statement: Κρονίων, the son of Cronus (Zeus), fixes rainbows in a cloud (στήριξε, aorist of στηρίζω) as a portent. The meaning of μερόπων in μερόπων ἀνθρώπων is not known; the ancient explanation, ‘with divided speech’, i.e. articulate, is followed here, and ‘mortal’ is the other guess.

sentences.t: ἀμφὶ δ’ ἄρ’ ὤμοισιν βάλετο ξίφος·
sentences.l: and about his shoulders he slung the sword;
sentences.i: and he slung the sword about his shoulders;
sentences.n: ἀμφὶ … βάλετο is tmesis, ‘threw about himself’, ‘slung on’; ὤμοισιν is the epic dative plural of ὦμος ‘shoulder’, and ἄρα is a connecting particle. The sword hangs from a strap, as the next lines show. The line has the words of Paris’ arming (3.334) apart from the silver-studded epithet, which is not here, and ‘slung’ is kept from there.

sentences.t:
ἐν δέ οἱ ἧλοι
χρύσειοι πάμφαινον, ἀτὰρ περὶ κουλεὸν ἦεν
ἀργύρεον χρυσέοισιν ἀορτήρεσσιν ἀρηρός.
sentences.l:
and on it studs
golden shone all-bright, and about it was a sheath
of silver, with golden straps fitted.
sentences.i: Golden studs shone all over it, and about it was a silver sheath, fitted with golden straps.
sentences.n: ἐν … οἱ is ‘on it’, the sword. ἧλοι are studs or rivets (the Greek does not say which part of the sword); χρύσειοι ‘golden’ agrees with them, and πάμφαινον ‘shone all over’ is built on παν- + φαίνω. περὶ … ἦεν is tmesis for ‘was about it’ (ἦεν = ἦν), with κουλεόν ‘sheath’ its subject and ἀργύρεον ‘of silver’; ἀρηρός, a perfect-participle form of ἀραρίσκω whose formation and gender are not certain, is ‘fitted’, and ἀορτήρεσσιν are the straps from which the sword hung (epic dative plural in -εσσιν).

sentences.t:
ἂν δ’ ἕλετ’ ἀμφιβρότην πολυδαίδαλον ἀσπίδα θοῦριν
καλήν, ἣν πέρι μὲν κύκλοι δέκα χάλκεοι ἦσαν,
ἐν δέ οἱ ὀμφαλοὶ ἦσαν ἐείκοσι κασσιτέροιο
λευκοί, ἐν δὲ μέσοισιν ἔην μέλανος κυάνοιο.
sentences.l:
And up he took the man-covering, much-wrought, impetuous shield,
fine, round which ten rings of bronze there were,
and on it bosses there were twenty, of tin,
white, and in the middle there was one of black kyanos.
sentences.i: He took up his man-covering shield, richly wrought and impetuous, a fine one, with ten rings of bronze round it, and twenty white bosses of tin on it, and in the middle one of black kyanos.
sentences.n: ἂν … ἕλετ’ is tmesis for ‘took up’. ἀμφιβρότην ‘man-covering’ is a shield big enough to cover the man; πολυδαίδαλον ‘richly wrought’ and θοῦριν ‘impetuous’ (a word for rushing, as in θοῦρος Ἄρης) agree with ἀσπίδα, and καλήν ‘fine’ follows at the start of the next line. ἣν πέρι is περὶ ἥν, the preposition set after its relative; κύκλοι are rings of bronze round the shield. ὀμφαλοί ‘bosses’ are the raised knobs, ἐείκοσι ‘twenty’, κασσιτέροιο ‘of tin’, λευκοί ‘white’. ἔην is a singular verb with no subject expressed: one boss, the middle one, of kyanos is understood (kyanos is explained at the breastplate).

sentences.t:
τῇ δ’ ἐπὶ μὲν Γοργὼ βλοσυρῶπις ἐστεφάνωτο
δεινὸν δερκομένη, περὶ δὲ Δεῖμός τε Φόβος τε.
sentences.l:
On it, upon, Gorgo grim-faced was set as a crown,
fearsomely looking, and about her Dread and Terror.
sentences.i: On it, like a crown, was set the grim-faced Gorgon, with her fearsome stare, and about her were Dread and Terror.
sentences.n: τῇ ‘on it’ is the shield, and ἐπί repeats ‘upon’ as an adverb. Γοργώ is the Gorgon, a monster, whose face is shown on the shield. ἐστεφάνωτο is the pluperfect passive of στεφανόω ‘crown’: she is set on the shield like a crown, but how the picture lay is not said. βλοσυρῶπις is built on ὤψ ‘face’, and the meaning of βλοσυρός is not certain (‘grim’ is the usual guess). δεινὸν δερκομένη is ‘looking fearsomely’, with δεινόν as an adverb. Δεῖμός and Φόβος are Dread and Terror, here figures on the shield, and περί as an adverb is ‘round about’ her. Line 37 is metrically irregular as transmitted: δέ in περὶ δὲ Δεῖμός stands at the start of the fourth foot, where it is short but must count long.

sentences.t: τῆς δ’ ἐξ ἀργύρεος τελαμὼν ἦν·
sentences.l: and from it a strap of silver there was;
sentences.i: and it had a strap of silver;
sentences.n: τῆς ‘of it’ is the shield, and τῆς δ’ ἐξ is ‘from it’, the preposition set after its pronoun. τελαμών is the strap that carries the shield from the shoulder, ἀργύρεος ‘of silver’. The unit is short because it stops at the raised dot, in the middle of the line.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπ’ αὐτοῦ
κυάνεος ἐλέλικτο δράκων, κεφαλαὶ δέ οἱ ἦσαν
τρεῖς ἀμφιστρεφέες ἑνὸς αὐχένος ἐκπεφυυῖαι.
sentences.l:
and upon it
a dark serpent was coiled, and heads to it there were
three, turning about, from one neck grown out.
sentences.i: and on the strap a dark serpent was coiled, and it had three heads turning about, growing out of one neck.
sentences.n: ἐπ’ αὐτοῦ ‘upon it’ is the strap (masculine like τελαμών; the shield is feminine). ἐλέλικτο is the pluperfect passive of ἐλελίζω ‘whirl’, here ‘was coiled’. κεφαλαὶ δέ οἱ ἦσαν is ‘and it had heads’, οἱ being the dative of possession. ἀμφιστρεφέες ‘turning about’ is built on ἀμφί + στρέφω; how the heads turned is not said. ἐκπεφυυῖαι is the perfect participle of ἐκφύω ‘grow out’, and ἑνὸς αὐχένος ‘from one neck’ is a genitive of the source.

sentences.t:
κρατὶ δ’ ἐπ’ ἀμφίφαλον κυνέην θέτο τετραφάληρον
ἵππουριν·
sentences.l:
And on his head he set the two-ridged helmet, four-ridged,
horse-tailed;
sentences.i: On his head he set the helmet, two-ridged and four-ridged, with its horsetail plume;
sentences.n: κρατὶ δ’ ἐπ’ … θέτο is tmesis, ‘set on his head’, with κρατί the epic dative of κάρη ‘head’ and θέτο the unaugmented aorist middle of τίθημι; κυνέην is the helmet. ἀμφίφαλον and τετραφάληρον are built on φάλος, usually taken as the ridge of a helmet; ‘two-ridged’ and ‘four-ridged’ are the literal readings, and what the helmet looked like is not known. ἵππουριν ‘horse-tailed’ is ἵππος + οὐρά, a crest of horsehair. The unit stops at the raised dot.

sentences.t: δεινὸν δὲ λόφος καθύπερθεν ἔνευεν.
sentences.l: and fearsomely the crest above nodded;
sentences.i: and fearsomely the crest nodded above;
sentences.n: λόφος is the horsehair crest, καθύπερθεν ‘above’ is where it stands, and ἔνευεν ‘nodded’ is the imperfect of νεύω with ἐν-. δεινόν is an adverb, ‘fearsomely’. The words are those of 3.337 in Paris’ arming and of an Odyssey line, and their English is kept.

sentences.t:
εἵλετο δ’ ἄλκιμα δοῦρε δύω κεκορυθμένα χαλκῷ
ὀξέα·
sentences.l:
and he took two sturdy spears, armed with bronze,
sharp;
sentences.i: and he took two sturdy spears, armed with bronze, sharp ones;
sentences.n: εἵλετο ‘took’ is the aorist middle of αἱρέω. δοῦρε is the dual of δόρυ ‘spear’, so with δύω ‘two’ it is a pair of spears. ἄλκιμα ‘sturdy’ is the stock epithet of spears, κεκορυθμένα, literally ‘helmeted’ (from κόρυς), agrees with δοῦρε and is ‘armed’, here ‘with bronze’, and ὀξέα ‘sharp’ falls at the start of the next line. The first line is also an Odyssey line, and its English is kept.

sentences.t:
τῆλε δὲ χαλκὸς ἀπ’ αὐτόφιν οὐρανὸν εἴσω
λάμπ’·
sentences.l:
and far off the bronze from them into heaven
shone;
sentences.i: and far off the bronze shone from them into heaven;
sentences.n: τῆλε ‘far off’ and χαλκός ‘bronze’ here mean the gleam from the spear-heads. αὐτόφιν has the old ending -φιν and means ‘from them’, the spears themselves. οὐρανὸν εἴσω is ‘into heaven’, the accusative of the place reached. λάμπ’ is ἔλαμπε, unaugmented and elided. The unit stops at the raised dot, in the middle of the line.

sentences.t:
ἐπὶ δ’ ἐγδούπησαν Ἀθηναίη τε καὶ Ἥρη
τιμῶσαι βασιλῆα πολυχρύσοιο Μυκήνης.
sentences.l:
and thereupon thundered Athena and Hera,
honouring the king of Mycenae rich in gold.
sentences.i: and thereupon Athena and Hera thundered, honouring the king of Mycenae rich in gold.
sentences.n: ἐπὶ δ’ ἐγδούπησαν is ‘and thereupon … thundered’: ἐγδούπησαν is from ἐγδουπέω ‘crash, thunder’ (perhaps ἐκ- + δουπέω, but the formation is not certain), and ἐπί is an adverb, ‘upon it’ or ‘in answer’. The Greek does not say how the goddesses made the noise, only that it honoured Agamemnon: τιμῶσαι is the feminine participle ‘honouring’. βασιλῆα … Μυκήνης calls him by his city, and πολυχρύσοιο ‘rich in gold’ is its stock epithet; Μυκήνης is the genitive of Μυκήνη.

sentences.t:
ἡνιόχῳ μὲν ἔπειτα ἑῷ ἐπέτελλεν ἕκαστος
ἵππους εὖ κατὰ κόσμον ἐρυκέμεν αὖθ’ ἐπὶ τάφρῳ,
sentences.l:
To his charioteer, then, his own, gave orders each man,
the horses well in due order to hold back there at the ditch,
sentences.i: Then each man ordered his own charioteer to hold the horses back there at the ditch, in good order,
sentences.n: ἡνιόχῳ … ἑῷ: ἑός is the possessive ‘his own’ (not an article), and ἕκαστος ‘each one’ is each of the leaders. ἐπέτελλεν, ‘gave orders to’, takes the dative, so the charioteer is told to hold the horses back (ἐρυκέμεν, the epic infinitive of ἐρύκω). εὖ κατὰ κόσμον is ‘well in due order’; αὖθ’ is αὖθι ‘right there’; τάφρῳ is ‘ditch’. The μέν here is answered by αὐτοὶ δέ in the next unit.

sentences.t:
αὐτοὶ δὲ πρυλέες σὺν τεύχεσι θωρηχθέντες
ῥώοντ’·
sentences.l:
but they themselves, the foot-soldiers, with their armour armed,
rushed on;
sentences.i: while the men themselves, the foot-soldiers, armed in their armour, rushed forward;
sentences.n: αὐτοὶ δέ ‘but they themselves’ answers ἡνιόχῳ μέν: the charioteers hold the horses, and the men go on foot. πρυλέες ‘foot-soldiers’ are the men fighting on foot; θωρηχθέντες is the aorist passive participle of θωρήσσω ‘arm with a breastplate’ (θώραξ), so ‘armed’, and σὺν τεύχεσι is ‘with their armour’. ῥώοντ’ is ἐρρώοντο, the imperfect of ῥώομαι ‘rush, move swiftly’, without augment. The unit stops at the raised dot, in the middle of the line.

sentences.t: ἄσβεστος δὲ βοὴ γένετ’ ἠῶθι πρό.
sentences.l: and unquenchable a shout arose early in the morning.
sentences.i: and a shout that would never go out arose in the early morning.
sentences.n: ἄσβεστος ‘unquenchable’ is literally ‘that cannot be put out’, a word from fire, so the English keeps the image of a flame that does not die. βοή is the battle-shout, and γένετ’ is ἐγένετο, unaugmented. ἠῶθι πρό is ‘early in the morning’; ἠῶθι is built on ἠώς ‘dawn’, and the exact force of πρό ‘before’ in the phrase is not clear.

sentences.t:
φθὰν δὲ μέγ’ ἱππήων ἐπὶ τάφρῳ κοσμηθέντες,
ἱππῆες δ’ ὀλίγον μετεκίαθον·
sentences.l:
And they were far ahead of the horsemen, at the ditch drawn up in order,
and the horsemen a little after went;
sentences.i: The foot-soldiers got to the ditch far ahead of the horsemen and stood drawn up in order, and the horsemen followed a little behind;
sentences.n: φθὰν is the unaugmented aorist 3 pl. of φθάνω ‘get in front, be first’ (Attic ἔφθασαν), with μέγα ‘greatly’, and the genitive ἱππήων is the comparison, ‘ahead of the horsemen’. The subject is the foot-soldiers named in the last unit. κοσμηθέντες is the aorist passive participle of κοσμέω ‘put in order’, from the same κόσμος as ‘due order’ above. ἱππῆες are ‘horsemen’, here the fighters who go in chariots, and μετεκίαθον is a rare form meaning ‘went after’. The unit stops at the raised dot, in the middle of the line.

sentences.t:
ἐν δὲ κυδοιμὸν
ὦρσε κακὸν Κρονίδης, κατὰ δ’ ὑψόθεν ἧκεν ἐέρσας
αἵματι μυδαλέας ἐξ αἰθέρος,
sentences.l:
and among them an uproar
evil raised the son of Cronus, and down from on high sent dewdrops
wet with blood from the upper air,
sentences.i: and the son of Cronus stirred up an evil uproar among them, and sent down from on high, out of the upper air, dewdrops wet with blood,
sentences.n: ἐν … ὦρσε is tmesis for ‘stirred up among (them)’, ὦρσε the aorist of ὄρνυμι; κυδοιμός is ‘uproar’, the din of battle, and Κρονίδης ‘son of Cronus’ is Zeus. κατά … ἧκεν is tmesis again, ‘sent down’ (the aorist of ἵημι), and ὑψόθεν is ‘from on high’. ἐέρσας is the accusative plural of ἔρση ‘dew’, so ‘dewdrops’, and αἵματι μυδαλέας is ‘wet with blood’ (μυδαλέος ‘damp’, with the dative of what wets them). αἰθήρ is the upper air. The next unit says why.

sentences.t:
οὕνεκ’ ἔμελλε
πολλὰς ἰφθίμους κεφαλὰς Ἄϊδι προϊάψειν.
sentences.l:
because he was about
many mighty heads to Hades to send forth.
sentences.i: because he was about to fling many mighty heads down to Hades.
sentences.n: The subject is still Zeus. οὕνεκ’ ἔμελλε is ‘because he was about to’, with the future infinitive προϊάψειν ‘to send forth, to fling’; κεφαλάς ‘heads’ stands for the men themselves, and ἰφθίμους ‘mighty’ is the stock epithet. Ἄϊδι is the dative of Ἄϊς, a by-form of Ἅιδης ‘Hades’.

sentences.t:
Τρῶες δ’ αὖθ’ ἑτέρωθεν ἐπὶ θρωσμῷ πεδίοιο
Ἕκτορά τ’ ἀμφὶ μέγαν καὶ ἀμύμονα Πουλυδάμαντα
Αἰνείαν θ’, ὃς Τρωσὶ θεὸς ὣς τίετο δήμῳ,
sentences.l:
And the Trojans, in turn, on the other side, on the rising ground of the plain
(were drawn up) around Hector, great, and blameless Polydamas,
and Aeneas, who among the Trojans like a god was honoured in the land,
sentences.i: And on the other side the Trojans were drawn up on the rising ground of the plain, around great Hector and blameless Polydamas and Aeneas, who among the Trojans was honoured like a god in the land,
sentences.n: The sentence has no verb in Greek; something like ‘were drawn up’ is understood, and the English supplies it (in parentheses in the literal layer). αὖθ’ is αὖτε ‘in turn’, ἑτέρωθεν ‘from the other side’, and ἐπὶ θρωσμῷ πεδίοιο ‘on the rising ground of the plain’ (a θρωσμός is a rise, from θρῴσκω ‘leap’). Ἕκτορά τ’ ἀμφὶ μέγαν has ἀμφί set after its noun, ‘around great Hector’. The meaning of ἀμύμονα, here of Polydamas (Πουλυδάμαντα), is not known; ‘blameless’ is the usual guess. Αἰνείαν is Aeneas, and θεὸς ὣς τίετο δήμῳ ‘was honoured like a god in the land’ is a formula whose English is kept.

sentences.t:
τρεῖς τ’ Ἀντηνορίδας Πόλυβον καὶ Ἀγήνορα δῖον
ἠΐθεόν τ’ Ἀκάμαντ’ ἐπιείκελον ἀθανάτοισιν.
sentences.l:
and the three Antenor’s-sons, Polybus and Agenor, heavenly,
and the young man Acamas, resembling the immortals.
sentences.i: and the three sons of Antenor, Polybus and heavenly Agenor and the young man Acamas, who was like the immortals.
sentences.n: τρεῖς … Ἀντηνορίδας is ‘the three sons of Antenor’ (a patronymic in the plural), and the names that follow are in apposition: Polybus, Agenor and Acamas. δῖον ‘heavenly’ is the stock epithet, here of Agenor. ἠΐθεον is ‘young man’ (the word is also used of an unmarried youth), and ἐπιείκελον ἀθανάτοισιν ‘like the immortals’ is an epithet with the dative of what he is like.

sentences.t: Ἕκτωρ δ’ ἐν πρώτοισι φέρ’ ἀσπίδα πάντοσ’ ἐΐσην,
sentences.l: And Hector among the foremost bore a shield equal on every side,
sentences.i: Hector carried, among the foremost, a shield equal on every side,
sentences.n: φέρ’ is ἔφερε ‘carried’, unaugmented and elided, and ἐν πρώτοισι is ‘among the foremost’, the front fighters. πάντοσ’ ἐΐσην ‘equal on every side’ says the shield was round and balanced. The comma leaves the sentence open for the comparison that follows.

sentences.t:
οἷος δ’ ἐκ νεφέων ἀναφαίνεται οὔλιος ἀστὴρ
παμφαίνων, τοτὲ δ’ αὖτις ἔδυ νέφεα σκιόεντα,
sentences.l:
and as from the clouds appears a ruinous star,
all-shining, and then again goes into the shadowy clouds,
sentences.i: and as a ruinous star shows itself from out of the clouds, all-shining, and then goes again into the shadowy clouds,
sentences.n: οἷος δέ begins the comparison, ‘and as’ (a star such as …). ἀναφαίνεται ‘shows itself’ is a present, and ἔδυ a general aorist, ‘goes’, the tense for what always happens. The Greek does not name the star. οὔλιος is a longer form of οὖλος ‘ruinous’ (as in οὖλος Ἄρης), and ‘ruinous’ is the house word; παμφαίνων is ‘all-shining’, and νέφεα σκιόεντα ‘shadowy clouds’ (νέφεα the uncontracted plural of νέφος).

sentences.t:
ὣς Ἕκτωρ ὁτὲ μέν τε μετὰ πρώτοισι φάνεσκεν,
ἄλλοτε δ’ ἐν πυμάτοισι κελεύων·
sentences.l:
so Hector at one time among the foremost would appear,
at another among the last, bidding;
sentences.i: so Hector would appear at one time among the foremost and at another among the last, giving orders;
sentences.n: ὣς … ὁτὲ μέν … ἄλλοτε δέ is ‘so … at one time … at another’, closing the comparison; τε after ὁτὲ μέν is an epic filler. φάνεσκεν is an iterative in -σκ- (a past tense with no augment), ‘would appear’, which is the point: Hector kept going back and forth. πυμάτοισι is the epic dative plural of πύματος ‘last’, and κελεύων ‘bidding’ says he gave the orders. The unit stops at the raised dot, in the middle of the line.

sentences.t:
πᾶς δ’ ἄρα χαλκῷ
λάμφ’ ὥς τε στεροπὴ πατρὸς Διὸς αἰγιόχοιο.
sentences.l:
and all in bronze
he shone like the lightning of father Zeus, aegis-bearing.
sentences.i: and he shone all over in his bronze, like the lightning of aegis-bearing father Zeus.
sentences.n: πᾶς δ’ ἄρα χαλκῷ is ‘and all in bronze’, the dative being of means. λάμφ’ is ἔλαμπε, elided before ὥς, whose rough breathing turns π into φ. στεροπή is a ‘flash’ of lightning, πατρὸς Διός ‘of father Zeus’, and αἰγιόχοιο ‘aegis-bearing’, the stock epithet, is the epic genitive in -οιο.

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’, ὥς τ’ ἀμητῆρες ἐναντίοι ἀλλήλοισιν
ὄγμον ἐλαύνωσιν ἀνδρὸς μάκαρος κατ’ ἄρουραν
πυρῶν ἢ κριθῶν·
sentences.i: And they, as reapers who face one another drive a swath along the plough-land of a blessed man, of wheat or barley,
sentences.n: οἳ δ’ ‘and they’ are the two armies; the sentence begins with them and turns at once to the comparison, so the main clause comes only at ὣς Τρῶες, two units on. ὥς τ’ is ‘as’, and ἐλαύνωσιν is a subjunctive without ἄν, as often in similes. An ὄγμος is a swath, the line of cut stalks; ἐναντίοι ἀλλήλοισιν ‘face to face with one another’ describes the reapers coming at each other. ἀνδρὸς μάκαρος is ‘of a blessed man’, here simply a prosperous one, and κατ’ ἄρουραν ‘along the plough-land’; πυρῶν ἢ κριθῶν is ‘of wheat or of barley’. The unit stops at the raised dot.

sentences.t: τὰ δὲ δράγματα ταρφέα πίπτει·
sentences.l: and the handfuls thick fall;
sentences.i: and the handfuls of grain fall thick;
sentences.n: δράγματα are handfuls of cut stalks, and ταρφέα ‘thick’ (close together) agrees with them. πίπτει is singular because a neuter plural subject takes a singular verb in Greek.

sentences.t:
ὣς Τρῶες καὶ Ἀχαιοὶ ἐπ’ ἀλλήλοισι θορόντες
δῄουν, οὐδ’ ἕτεροι μνώοντ’ ὀλοοῖο φόβοιο.
sentences.l:
so Trojans and Achaeans, upon one another having leapt,
cut down, and neither side thought of baneful flight.
sentences.i: so Trojans and Achaeans leapt upon one another and cut each other down, and neither side gave a thought to baneful flight.
sentences.n: ὣς … is the main clause the comparison was waiting for. θορόντες is the aorist participle of θρῴσκω ‘leap’, and ἐπ’ ἀλλήλοισι is ‘upon one another’. δῄουν is the imperfect of δηϊόω ‘cut down’ without the augment (Attic ἐδῄουν), and no object is stated; ‘one another’ is understood. οὐδ’ ἕτεροι, literally ‘nor the others’, is ‘neither side’. μνώοντ’ is ἐμνώοντο, the imperfect of μνάομαι ‘be mindful of’, with the genitive ὀλοοῖο φόβοιο; ὀλοός is ‘baneful’, and φόβος here is ‘flight’, not the figure Terror of the shield.

sentences.t:
ἴσας δ’ ὑσμίνη κεφαλὰς ἔχεν, οἳ δὲ λύκοι ὣς
θῦνον·
sentences.l:
And equal heads the battle held, and they like wolves
rushed;
sentences.i: The battle held their heads level, and they rushed on like wolves;
sentences.n: ὑσμίνη ‘battle’ is the subject. ἴσας … κεφαλάς, literally ‘equal heads’, is an idiom that the Greek does not explain; the usual sense is that the fighting kept the two sides level, but the exact picture is not known. ἔχεν is ἔχε with movable ν. λύκοι ὣς is ‘like wolves’, the ὥς set after its noun, and θῦνον is the imperfect of θύνω ‘rush, dart’. The unit stops at the raised dot, in the middle of the line.

sentences.t: Ἔρις δ’ ἄρ’ ἔχαιρε πολύστονος εἰσορόωσα·
sentences.l: and Strife then rejoiced, the much-groaning, looking on;
sentences.i: and Strife, of the many groans, rejoiced as she looked on;
sentences.n: Ἔρις is the goddess Zeus sent at 11.3. ἄρ’ is ‘then’, a particle of natural sequence. πολύστονος means literally ‘of many groans’; of Strife it is taken as ‘causing many groans’. εἰσορόωσα is the uncontracted feminine participle of εἰσοράω ‘look on’ (Attic εἰσορῶσα), and the unit stops at the raised dot.

sentences.t: οἴη γάρ ῥα θεῶν παρετύγχανε μαρναμένοισιν,
sentences.l: for alone of the gods she was present with them as they fought,
sentences.i: for she alone of the gods was present with the men as they fought,
sentences.n: οἴη is the feminine of οἶος ‘alone’, ‘she alone’, and γάρ ῥα gives the reason for her joy. παρετύγχανε is the imperfect of παρατυγχάνω ‘happen to be present’, and μαρναμένοισιν the dative plural of the participle of μάρναμαι ‘fight’, agreeing with an unstated ‘them’, the fighting men.

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ ἄλλοι οὔ σφιν πάρεσαν θεοί, ἀλλὰ ἕκηλοι
σφοῖσιν ἐνὶ μεγάροισι καθήατο, ἧχι ἑκάστῳ
δώματα καλὰ τέτυκτο κατὰ πτύχας Οὐλύμποιο.
sentences.l:
but the other gods were not present with them, but at ease
in their own halls they were sitting, where to each
houses fair had been made along the folds of Olympus.
sentences.i: But the other gods were not with them; they sat at ease in their own halls, where each had a fair house made for him along the folds of Olympus.
sentences.n: οἳ δ’ ἄλλοι … θεοί is ‘the others, the gods’ (οἳ is the article as pronoun). πάρεσαν is the epic imperfect of πάρειμι ‘be present’, σφιν ‘with them’ is the fighting men, and ἕκηλοι is ‘at ease’. σφοῖσιν is the possessive ‘their own’, not the article. καθήατο is the epic imperfect of κάθημαι ‘sit’, with -ατο for -ντο. ἧχι ‘where’ is an epic relative adverb. τέτυκτο is the pluperfect passive of τεύχω ‘make’, ‘had been made’, with ἑκάστῳ ‘for each’; πτύχας Οὐλύμποιο are ‘the folds of Olympus’, its ridges and valleys.

sentences.t:
πάντες δ’ ᾐτιόωντο κελαινεφέα Κρονίωνα
οὕνεκ’ ἄρα Τρώεσσιν ἐβούλετο κῦδος ὀρέξαι.
sentences.l:
And all blamed the dark-clouded son of Cronus
because to the Trojans he wished to grant glory.
sentences.i: All of them blamed the son of Cronus of the dark clouds, because he wished to grant glory to the Trojans.
sentences.n: ᾐτιόωντο is the uncontracted imperfect of αἰτιάομαι ‘blame’ (Attic ᾐτιῶντο). κελαινεφέα Κρονίωνα is ‘the dark-clouded son of Cronus’ (Zeus), and Κρονίων is a second patronymic, beside Κρονίδης. ἐβούλετο is ‘wished’, and ὀρέξαι is the aorist infinitive of ὀρέγω ‘reach out, hold out’, so ‘grant’ with κῦδος; Τρώεσσιν ἐβούλετο κῦδος ὀρέξαι is also an Odyssey half-line, and its English is kept; κῦδος ‘glory’ is the glory a god gives in battle, and Τρώεσσιν is the epic dative plural.

sentences.t: τῶν μὲν ἄρ’ οὐκ ἀλέγιζε πατήρ·
sentences.l: Of them, then, did not care the father;
sentences.i: But the father did not care about them;
sentences.n: τῶν ‘of them’ are the gods who blamed him, and πατήρ ‘the father’ is Zeus, without further name. ἀλέγιζε is the imperfect of ἀλεγίζω ‘care for’, which takes the genitive. The μέν is answered by ὃ δέ in the next unit. The unit stops at the raised dot, in the middle of the line.

sentences.t:
ὃ δὲ νόσφι λιασθεὶς
τῶν ἄλλων ἀπάνευθε καθέζετο κύδεϊ γαίων
εἰσορόων Τρώων τε πόλιν καὶ νῆας Ἀχαιῶν
χαλκοῦ τε στεροπήν, ὀλλύντάς τ’ ὀλλυμένους τε.
sentences.l:
but he, withdrawn apart
from the others, apart sat down, exulting in glory,
looking on the city of the Trojans and the ships of the Achaeans
and the flash of bronze, those destroying and those perishing.
sentences.i: He withdrew from the others and sat down far apart, exulting in his glory, looking out on the city of the Trojans and the ships of the Achaeans, on the flash of bronze, and on the men who killed and the men who were killed.
sentences.n: ὃ δέ ‘but he’ answers the μέν before it. νόσφι λιασθείς is the aorist passive participle of λιάζομαι ‘withdraw’ with νόσφι ‘apart’, and τῶν ἄλλων ἀπάνευθε is ‘apart from the others’. The words from καθέζετο ‘sat down’ through Ἀχαιῶν at the end of 11.82 are those of 8.51–52, and their English is kept. χαλκοῦ τε στεροπήν is ‘the flash of bronze’. The last two words are participles of ὄλλυμι, active ὀλλύντας ‘destroying’ and middle ὀλλυμένους ‘perishing’ (so ‘killing’ and ‘being killed’), joined by τε … τε.

sentences.t: ὄφρα μὲν ἠὼς ἦν καὶ ἀέξετο ἱερὸν ἦμαρ,
sentences.l: As long as it was morning and the sacred day was growing,
sentences.i: For as long as it was morning and the sacred day was growing,
sentences.n: ὄφρα … τόφρα ‘as long as … for that long’ pairs this clause with the next. ἠώς is ‘dawn, morning’, and ἀέξετο ‘was growing’ is the imperfect middle of ἀέξω, without augment. ἱερὸν ἦμαρ ‘the sacred day’ is the formula for the daylight. These two lines stand at 8.66–67, and their English is kept.

sentences.t: τόφρα μάλ’ ἀμφοτέρων βέλε’ ἥπτετο, πῖπτε δὲ λαός·
sentences.l: for that time the missiles of both sides took hold, and the people fell.
sentences.i: for that time the missiles of both sides struck home, and the army fell.
sentences.n: τόφρα ‘for that long’ answers ὄφρα. ἥπτετο, the imperfect of ἅπτομαι ‘take hold’, is said of missiles that find their mark, and βέλε’ is βέλεα, the uncontracted plural of βέλος ‘missile’. λαός ‘people’ is the army, the men of both sides, and the English layer says ‘army’. The unit stops at the raised dot; the same words stand at 8.67 with a full stop.

sentences.t:
ἦμος δὲ δρυτόμος περ ἀνὴρ ὁπλίσσατο δεῖπνον
οὔρεος ἐν βήσσῃσιν,
sentences.l:
And at the time when a woodcutter man makes ready his meal
in the glens of a mountain,
sentences.i: And at the time when a woodcutter makes ready his meal in the glens of a mountain,
sentences.n: ἦμος ‘at the time when’ opens a long time-clause that names the hour by what a woodcutter does; the main clause is τῆμος ‘at that time’, four lines later (11.90). περ, after δρυτόμος, is an emphatic particle that the English leaves untranslated. δρυτόμος ἀνήρ is ‘a woodcutter’ (δρῦς ‘oak, tree’ + τέμνω ‘cut’). ὁπλίσσατο is a general aorist, ‘makes ready’, and δεῖπνον is ‘meal’. οὔρεος is the epic genitive of ὄρος ‘mountain’, and βήσσῃσιν the epic dative plural of βῆσσα ‘glen, wooded valley’.

sentences.t:
ἐπεί τ’ ἐκορέσσατο χεῖρας
τάμνων δένδρεα μακρά, ἅδος τέ μιν ἵκετο θυμόν,
σίτου τε γλυκεροῖο περὶ φρένας ἵμερος αἱρεῖ,
sentences.l:
when he has sated his hands
of cutting tall trees, and weariness has come on his heart,
and for sweet food about his wits longing takes hold,
sentences.i: when he has had his fill of cutting tall trees, and weariness has come on his heart, and longing for sweet food takes hold of his wits,
sentences.n: ἐκορέσσατο χεῖρας is literally ‘he has satisfied his hands’, the aorist middle of κορέννυμι with χεῖρας as accusative of the part: he has had enough of the work. τάμνων is the participle of τάμνω (Ionic for τέμνω) ‘cut’, and δένδρεα μακρά ‘tall trees’. ἅδος is ‘satiety, weariness’, and μιν … θυμόν is ‘him in his heart’. σίτου … γλυκεροῖο is ‘of sweet food’, ἵμερος ‘longing’ is the subject, and περὶ φρένας … αἱρεῖ is ‘takes about the wits’ (tmesis). The tenses are general, as in a simile.

sentences.t:
τῆμος σφῇ ἀρετῇ Δαναοὶ ῥήξαντο φάλαγγας
κεκλόμενοι ἑτάροισι κατὰ στίχας·
sentences.l:
then by their own excellence the Danaans broke the battle-lines,
calling to their companions along the ranks;
sentences.i: then the Danaans broke the battle-lines by their own excellence, calling to their companions along the ranks;
sentences.n: τῆμος ‘then’ answers ἦμος and gives the main clause at last. σφῇ is the possessive ‘their own’ (not the article), and ἀρετῇ ‘excellence’, the dative of means, is here excellence in fighting. Δαναοί ‘Danaans’ is the poet’s name for the army here. ῥήξαντο is the aorist middle of ῥήγνυμι ‘break’, φάλαγγας are battle-lines, and κεκλόμενοι ‘calling’ is a reduplicated participle of κέλομαι. ἑτάροισι is the epic dative plural of ἕταρος ‘companion’, and κατὰ στίχας is ‘along the ranks’. The unit stops at the raised dot, in the middle of the line.

sentences.t:
ἐν δ’ Ἀγαμέμνων
πρῶτος ὄρουσ’, ἕλε δ’ ἄνδρα Βιάνορα ποιμένα λαῶν
αὐτόν, ἔπειτα δ’ ἑταῖρον Ὀϊλῆα πλήξιππον.
sentences.l:
and in among them Agamemnon
first sprang, and he took a man, Bianor, shepherd of the people,
himself, and then his companion Oileus, horse-lashing.
sentences.i: Agamemnon was the first to leap in among them, and he killed Bianor, shepherd of the people, and then Bianor’s companion Oileus, the horse-lasher.
sentences.n: ἐν … ὄρουσ’ is tmesis, ‘sprang in’, and ὄρουσ’ is the unaugmented aorist of ὀρούω ‘spring, rush’. ἕλε ‘took’ means ‘killed’ in a fight. ἄνδρα Βιάνορα is ‘a man, Bianor’, and αὐτόν ‘himself’ sets Bianor against his companion, who is killed next. ποιμένα λαῶν ‘shepherd of the people’ is the stock phrase for a leader. ἑταῖρον is ‘companion’, here Bianor’s (αὐτόν has just set him apart) and not Agamemnon’s, Ὀϊλῆα the accusative of Oileus, a Trojan, and πλήξιππον ‘horse-lashing’ (πλήσσω + ἵππος) his stock epithet, ‘the horse-lasher’.

sentences.t: ἤτοι ὅ γ’ ἐξ ἵππων κατεπάλμενος ἀντίος ἔστη·
sentences.l: He indeed, from the horses having leapt down, stood face to face;
sentences.i: Oileus, for his part, sprang down from his horses and stood facing him;
sentences.n: ἤτοι (one word in this edition) ‘indeed’, and ὅ γ’ ‘he for his part’ is the man named last. Bianor is already dead, so the one who comes down is Oileus, his companion. ἐξ ἵππων is ‘from the horses’, from his chariot; κατεπάλμενος is the syncopated aorist participle (like ἅλμενος) of ἅλλομαι ‘leap’, compounded with κατά and ἐπί, so ‘leaping down’, and ἀντίος ἔστη ‘stood opposite’ (ἔστη the aorist of ἵστημι). The unit stops at the raised dot.

sentences.t:
τὸν δ’ ἰθὺς μεμαῶτα μετώπιον ὀξέϊ δουρὶ
νύξ’,
sentences.l:
Him, straight at him eager, in the forehead with a sharp spear
he stabbed,
sentences.i: As he rushed straight at him, Agamemnon stabbed him in the forehead with his sharp spear,
sentences.n: τόν ‘him’ is Oileus, the object of νύξ’ (νύξε, the aorist of νύσσω ‘stab’, unaugmented and elided); the subject, Agamemnon, is not restated. ἰθύς is an adverb ‘straight (at him)’, and μεμαῶτα, the accusative participle of μέμαα, ‘eager, rushing’, agrees with τόν. μετώπιον is ‘in the forehead’ and ὀξέϊ δουρί ‘with sharp spear’ (δουρί the epic dative of δόρυ). The sentence runs on after the comma.

sentences.t:
οὐδὲ στεφάνη δόρυ οἱ σχέθε χαλκοβάρεια,
ἀλλὰ δι’ αὐτῆς ἦλθε καὶ ὀστέου, ἐγκέφαλος δὲ
ἔνδον ἅπας πεπάλακτο·
sentences.i: and the rim, heavy with bronze, did not hold the spear back for him; it went right through it and through the bone, and all the brain within was spattered about;
sentences.n: στεφάνη is the rim of the helmet (or its brow-band), and χαλκοβάρεια ‘heavy with bronze’ says it was made of bronze. οἱ ‘for him’ goes with σχέθε, the aorist of ἔχω ‘hold back’. ἀλλὰ δι’ αὐτῆς ἦλθε καὶ ὀστέου is ‘but through it went, and through bone’: the spear is the subject of ἦλθε, and the genitives go with δια-. ἐγκέφαλος ‘brain’ is the subject of the pluperfect passive πεπάλακτο, from παλάσσω ‘spatter’, and ἔνδον ἅπας is ‘within, all of it’. The unit stops at the raised dot, in the middle of the line.

sentences.t: δάμασσε δέ μιν μεμαῶτα.
sentences.l: and he subdued him, eager as he was.
sentences.i: and so he overcame him as he charged.
sentences.n: δάμασσε is the unaugmented aorist of δαμάζω ‘subdue’, ‘overcome’; the subject is Agamemnon and μιν is Oileus, and the result, the brain spattered, is death. μεμαῶτα is the same participle ‘eager, rushing’ as above, now ending the picture of a man who ran onto the spear.

sentences.t:
καὶ τοὺς μὲν λίπεν αὖθι ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν Ἀγαμέμνων
στήθεσι παμφαίνοντας, ἐπεὶ περίδυσε χιτῶνας·
sentences.l:
And these he left there, the lord of men, Agamemnon,
their chests all-shining, when he had stripped off their tunics;
sentences.i: Agamemnon, lord of men, left the two of them there, their chests all-shining now that he had stripped off their tunics;
sentences.n: τοὺς μέν ‘these’ are the two just killed, Bianor and Oileus. λίπεν is the unaugmented aorist of λείπω ‘leave’, and αὖθι ‘right there’. ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν Ἀγαμέμνων is ‘Agamemnon, lord of men’, the house rendering of the title. στήθεσι παμφαίνοντας is ‘shining at the chest’ (στήθεσι the epic dative plural, of respect), παμφαίνοντας ‘all-shining’ agreeing with τούς: with the tunics gone, bare skin shows. περίδυσε is the aorist of περιδύω ‘strip off all round’, and χιτῶνας are tunics. The unit stops at the raised dot.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ὃ βῆ Ἶσόν τε καὶ Ἄντιφον ἐξεναρίξων
υἷε δύω Πριάμοιο νόθον καὶ γνήσιον ἄμφω
εἰν ἑνὶ δίφρῳ ἐόντας·
sentences.i: Then he went to kill Isus and Antiphus and strip them of their armour, two sons of Priam, one illegitimate and one legitimate, both in one chariot;
sentences.n: αὐτὰρ ὃ βῆ is ‘but he went’ (βῆ the unaugmented aorist of βαίνω). Ἶσον and Ἄντιφον are the accusatives of Isus and Antiphus, and ἐξεναρίξων, the future participle of ἐξεναρίζω ‘kill and strip of the armour’ (ἐνάρα ‘spoils’), says why he went. υἷε δύω is the dual ‘two sons’; νόθον ‘bastard’ (in the reading layer ‘illegitimate’) and γνήσιον ‘true-born, legitimate’ are in apposition, and from the next lines the first is Isus. ἄμφω is ‘both’, εἰν is εἰνί = ἐν, and δίφρῳ is ‘chariot’. The unit stops at the raised dot, in the middle of the line.

sentences.t:
ὃ μὲν νόθος ἡνιόχευεν,
Ἄντιφος αὖ παρέβασκε περικλυτός·
sentences.l:
the one, the bastard, was driving,
Antiphus in turn stood beside, very famous;
sentences.i: the illegitimate one was driving, and Antiphus, very famous, stood beside him;
sentences.n: ὃ μὲν νόθος ‘the one, the bastard’ is Isus, whom this sentence does not name; ἡνιόχευεν ‘was driving’ comes from ἡνίοχος ‘charioteer’, ‘the holder of the reins’. Ἄντιφος αὖ is ‘Antiphus in turn’, and παρέβασκε ‘stood beside’ is the imperfect of a verb meaning ‘stand by’, the fighter next to the driver; the form is rare. περικλυτός ‘very famous’ is περι- ‘very’ + κλυτός ‘famous’. The unit stops at the raised dot, in the middle of the line.

sentences.t:
ὥ ποτ’ Ἀχιλλεὺς
Ἴδης ἐν κνημοῖσι δίδη μόσχοισι λύγοισι,
ποιμαίνοντ’ ἐπ’ ὄεσσι λαβών, καὶ ἔλυσεν ἀποίνων.
sentences.l:
whom, the two, once Achilles
in the spurs of Ida bound with young withies,
shepherding by the sheep having taken, and he released them for ransom.
sentences.i: Achilles had once caught the two of them herding sheep on the spurs of Ida, bound them with young withies, and then released them for a ransom.
sentences.n: ὥ is the dual relative, ‘whom, the two’, the object of δίδη and of λαβών. Ἴδης ἐν κνημοῖσι is ‘in the spurs of Ida’ (κνημός is a spur of a mountain, as κνήμη is the shin). δίδη is an epic reduplicated imperfect of δέω ‘bind’, and μόσχοισι λύγοισι ‘with young withies’ (a μόσχος is a young shoot, a λύγος a pliant twig). ποιμαίνοντ’ is the dual participle ‘shepherding’, elided, and ἐπ’ ὄεσσι ‘by the sheep’ (ὄεσσι the epic dative plural of ὄϊς); λαβών is ‘having taken them’, and ἔλυσεν ἀποίνων is ‘released for ransom’, ἀποίνων a genitive of price. The poet tells this earlier capture in passing.

sentences.t:
δὴ τότε γ’ Ἀτρεΐδης εὐρὺ κρείων Ἀγαμέμνων
τὸν μὲν ὑπὲρ μαζοῖο κατὰ στῆθος βάλε δουρί,
sentences.l:
Then indeed Atreus’-son, wide-ruling Agamemnon,
the one, above the nipple, in the chest struck with a spear,
sentences.i: Then the son of Atreus, wide-ruling Agamemnon, struck the one in the chest, above the nipple, with his spear,
sentences.n: δὴ τότε γ’ is ‘then indeed’. Ἀτρεΐδης … εὐρὺ κρείων Ἀγαμέμνων is ‘son of Atreus, wide-ruling Agamemnon’, εὐρύ (the adverb ‘widely’) and κρείων ‘ruling’ being printed as two words. τὸν μέν ‘the one’ is set against Ἄντιφον αὖ ‘Antiphus in turn’ in the next unit, so it is Isus. ὑπὲρ μαζοῖο is ‘above the nipple’, κατὰ στῆθος ‘in the chest’, and βάλε δουρί is ‘struck with a spear’.

sentences.t: Ἄντιφον αὖ παρὰ οὖς ἔλασε ξίφει, ἐκ δ’ ἔβαλ’ ἵππων.
sentences.l: Antiphus in turn beside the ear he struck with his sword, and out he threw from the horses.
sentences.i: and he struck Antiphus beside the ear with his sword and threw him from the horses.
sentences.n: παρὰ οὖς is ‘beside the ear’ (οὖς the accusative of the ear). ἔλασε is the aorist of ἐλαύνω ‘drive, strike’, and ξίφει the epic dative of ξίφος ‘sword’, the means. ἐκ … ἔβαλ’ is tmesis, ‘threw out’, and ἵππων ‘the horses’ is a genitive of separation: the pair of horses stands for the chariot.

sentences.t:
σπερχόμενος δ’ ἀπὸ τοῖιν ἐσύλα τεύχεα καλὰ
γιγνώσκων·
sentences.l:
And hastening, from the two he stripped their armour, fine,
recognising them;
sentences.i: Hurrying, he stripped the fine armour from the two of them, recognising them;
sentences.n: σπερχόμενος ‘hurrying’ is the participle of σπέρχομαι. ἀπὸ … ἐσύλα is tmesis, ‘stripped off’, and τοῖιν is the dual ‘from the two’; τεύχεα καλά is ‘fine armour’, and γιγνώσκων ‘recognising’ says he knows who they are. The unit stops at the raised dot, and the next explains how he knows them.

sentences.t:
καὶ γάρ σφε πάρος παρὰ νηυσὶ θοῇσιν
εἶδεν, ὅτ’ ἐξ Ἴδης ἄγαγεν πόδας ὠκὺς Ἀχιλλεύς.
sentences.l:
for indeed them before beside the swift ships
he had seen, when from Ida brought them swift-in-feet Achilles.
sentences.i: for he had seen them before, beside the swift ships, when Achilles, swift of foot, brought them from Ida.
sentences.n: καὶ γάρ is ‘for indeed’ and gives the reason for γιγνώσκων. σφε is the enclitic ‘them’, and πάρος ‘before’; εἶδεν is the aorist of ὁράω, ‘saw’, here ‘had seen’. θοῇσιν is the epic dative plural of θοός ‘swift’, the stock epithet of ships. ὅτ’ ἐξ Ἴδης ἄγαγεν is ‘when he brought them from Ida’, with ἄγαγεν the unaugmented aorist of ἄγω; πόδας ὠκὺς Ἀχιλλεύς is ‘Achilles, swift of foot’, the accusative πόδας being ‘in respect of the feet’.

sentences.t:
ὡς δὲ λέων ἐλάφοιο ταχείης νήπια τέκνα
ῥηϊδίως συνέαξε λαβὼν κρατεροῖσιν ὀδοῦσιν
ἐλθὼν εἰς εὐνήν, ἁπαλόν τέ σφ’ ἦτορ ἀπηύρα·
sentences.i: And as a lion that has come to the lair of a swift hind easily crushes her infant young, seizing them in his strong teeth, and takes their tender life away,
sentences.n: A second comparison. The Greek puts its verbs in the aorist (συνέαξε, ἀπηύρα), the aorist of a general truth, and the English uses the present. ἐλάφοιο ταχείης is ‘of a swift hind’ (a ἔλαφος is a deer, here a mother), and νήπια τέκνα ‘infant children’ are her fawns. συνέαξε is the aorist of συνάγνυμι ‘break together, crush’; ῥηϊδίως is ‘easily’, κρατεροῖσιν ὀδοῦσιν ‘strong teeth’. εὐνή is a bed, here the lair. ἀπηύρα is the unaugmented aorist of ἀπαυράω ‘take from’; ἦτορ is the ‘heart’ as the seat of life, so ‘took the tender heart from them’ means killed them, and σφ’ is σφι or σφε, ‘them’. The unit stops at the raised dot.

sentences.t:
ἣ δ’ εἴ πέρ τε τύχῃσι μάλα σχεδόν, οὐ δύναταί σφι
χραισμεῖν·
sentences.l:
And she, even if she happens to be very near, is not able for them
to avail;
sentences.i: and the hind, even if she happens to be very near, cannot help them;
sentences.n: ἣ δ’ ‘and she’ is the hind (ἥ, the article as pronoun). εἴ πέρ τε is ‘even if’, and τύχῃσι is the aorist subjunctive of τυγχάνω ‘happen to be’ with the epic ending -σι. μάλα σχεδόν is ‘very near’. χραισμεῖν ‘to avail, to help’ (it means to ward off harm) takes σφι ‘them’, the fawns’ dative; the same verb comes back at the end of the comparison. The unit stops at the raised dot, in the middle of the line.

sentences.t: αὐτὴν γάρ μιν ὑπὸ τρόμος αἰνὸς ἱκάνει·
sentences.l: for herself, upon her, from beneath fearsome trembling comes;
sentences.i: for fearsome trembling comes upon her herself, from beneath;
sentences.n: αὐτήν ‘her very self’ and μιν ‘her’ are doubled for emphasis. ὑπό is an adverb, ‘from beneath’, going with ἱκάνει (the Greek does not say where the trembling starts), the present of ἱκάνω, an epic by-form of ἱκνέομαι ‘come upon’. τρόμος is ‘trembling’ and αἰνός ‘fearsome’. The unit stops at the raised dot.

sentences.t:
καρπαλίμως δ’ ἤϊξε διὰ δρυμὰ πυκνὰ καὶ ὕλην
σπεύδουσ’ ἱδρώουσα κραταιοῦ θηρὸς ὑφ’ ὁρμῆς·
sentences.l:
and swiftly she darted through thick coppices and woodland,
hastening, sweating, under the onrush of the powerful beast;
sentences.i: and swiftly she darts through thick coppices and woodland, hastening, sweating, driven by the onrush of the powerful beast;
sentences.n: καρπαλίμως is ‘swiftly’; ἤϊξε is the aorist of ἀΐσσω ‘dart’, a general aorist like the earlier ones, and the English uses the present. διὰ δρυμὰ πυκνὰ καὶ ὕλην ‘through thick coppices and woodland’ is a half-line the Odyssey also has, and its English is kept. σπεύδουσ’ ἱδρώουσα are two participles, ‘hastening, sweating’ (ἱδρόω with diectasis). ὑφ’ ὁρμῆς is ‘under the onrush’, ὑπό with the genitive giving the cause. κραταιός ‘powerful’ is related to κράτος; it is rendered ‘powerful’ so that ‘mighty’ stays with ἴφθιμος and ‘strong’ with κρατερός.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἄρα τοῖς οὔ τις δύνατο χραισμῆσαι ὄλεθρον
Τρώων, ἀλλὰ καὶ αὐτοὶ ὑπ’ Ἀργείοισι φέβοντο.
sentences.l:
So then to them no one was able to ward off destruction
of the Trojans, but they themselves too before the Argives were fleeing.
sentences.i: So not one of the Trojans could ward off destruction from them, but they themselves were fleeing before the Argives.
sentences.n: ὣς ἄρα ‘so then’ closes the comparison: as the hind cannot help her young, none of the Trojans can help the two sons of Priam. τοῖς is ‘for them’, Isus and Antiphus. οὔ τις … Τρώων is ‘no one of the Trojans’, the genitive held to the start of the next line. δύνατο is the epic imperfect of δύναμαι ‘be able’, and χραισμῆσαι ὄλεθρον is ‘to ward off destruction’, the verb of χραισμεῖν above. ἀλλὰ καὶ αὐτοί ‘but they themselves too’ turns to the Trojan army; ὑπ’ Ἀργείοισι is ‘before the Argives’, ὑπό with the dative of the force that drives them, and φέβοντο the imperfect of φέβομαι ‘flee’.
